items.stem: Which is the definition of electric field strength at a point?
options: the work done per unit charge bringing a charge from infinity
the charge per unit area at the point
the force per unit positive charge on a small charge placed at the point
the force per unit mass at the point
items.answer: the force per unit positive charge on a small charge placed at the point
items.markingKey: E = F/q.

items.stem: Compare electric fields with gravitational fields, giving one similarity and one difference.
items.answer: Similarity: both are inverse-square fields for point sources / field strength defined as force per unit (charge/mass). Difference: gravitational forces are always attractive; electric forces can attract or repel.
items.markingKey: valid similarity [1]; valid difference [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the field lines near the surface of a charged conductor are perpendicular to the surface.
items.answer: If the field had a component along the surface, free charges would move; in equilibrium they do not, so the field must be perpendicular to the surface.
items.markingKey: parallel component would move charges [1]; static so perpendicular [1] [2]

items.stem: An electron is in a uniform electric field of strength 5.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Determine the magnitude of the electric force on it.
items.markingKey: F = qE = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5.0 × 10³ = 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁶ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An electron is in a uniform electric field of strength 1.2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Calculate the electric force on it and its acceleration (ignore gravity).

A small charged sphere carrying +2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C experiences a force of 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ N when placed at point P near a charged object. (a) Calculate the field strength at P. (b) Show that N C⁻¹ is equivalent to V m⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) 3.00 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ (b) V m⁻¹ = J C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N m C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N C⁻¹.
items.markingKey: (a) E = F/q (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.00 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) V = J C⁻¹ [1]; J = N m [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the unit of electric field strength?
items.answer: N C⁻¹
items.markingKey: E = F/q; equivalent to V m⁻¹.

items.stem: Describe the field pattern between two parallel plates with a p.d. between them, including the edges.
items.answer: Between the plates: parallel, equally spaced lines from + to − plate (uniform field); near the edges the lines curve outwards (edge effect).
items.markingKey: uniform parallel lines + to − [1]; curving at edges [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the force on a positive charge in an electric field is in the direction of the field lines.
items.answer: By definition field lines show the direction of the force on a small positive test charge.
items.markingKey: definition of field direction [1]; positive test charge [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the electric field pattern for an isolated negative point charge, and state what the spacing of the lines indicates.
items.answer: Radial lines pointing inwards, closer together near the charge; closer lines indicate a stronger field.
items.markingKey: correct shape [1]; correct direction [1]; spacing ↔ field strength [1] [3]

items.stem: A proton is in a uniform electric field of strength 1.2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Work out the magnitude of the electric force on it.
items.markingKey: F = qE = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.2 × 10⁴ = 1.92 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A dust particle with charge 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ C is in a uniform electric field of strength 1.2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Calculate the electric force on it and its acceleration (ignore gravity).

A small charged sphere carrying +2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C experiences a force of 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ N when placed at point P near a charged object. (a) Calculate the field strength at P. (b) The sphere is replaced by an electron. Calculate the force on the electron.
items.answer: (a) 2.00 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ (b) 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ N, in the opposite direction
items.markingKey: (a) E = F/q (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.00 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) F = eE [1]; opposite direction [1] [2]

items.stem: A small charged sphere carrying +5.0 × 10⁻⁹ C experiences a force of 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ N when placed at point P near a charged object. (a) Define electric field strength. (b) Calculate the field strength at P. (c) Show that N C⁻¹ is equivalent to V m⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) Force per unit positive charge on a small test charge. (b) 1.20 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ (c) V m⁻¹ = J C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N m C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N C⁻¹.
items.markingKey: (a) Force per unit positive charge on a small test charge [1] (b) E = F/q (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.20 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ [1] [2] (c) V = J C⁻¹ [1]; J = N m [1] [2]

items.stem: Two parallel plates 2.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 500 V between them. What is the field strength between them?
Explain why the path of an electron moving horizontally into the uniform vertical field between two charged plates is parabolic.
items.answer: The force eE is constant and vertical, so there is constant vertical acceleration; the horizontal velocity is constant (no horizontal force). This is the same as projectile motion, giving a parabola.
items.markingKey: constant vertical force/acceleration [1]; constant horizontal velocity → parabola [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the kinetic energy gained by a charge accelerated through a p.d. does not depend on the separation of the plates.
items.answer: Work done = qV; a larger separation gives a smaller field (E = V/d) but a longer distance, so qEd = qV is the same.
items.markingKey: W = qV [1]; E smaller but distance larger [1] [2]

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 4.0 cm apart with a p.d. of 200 V between them. An electron is between the plates. Determine the electric field strength between the plates.
items.markingKey: E = V/d = 200/0.040 = 5000 V m⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 1.0 cm apart with a p.d. of 600 V between them. An electron is between the plates. Calculate the field strength, the force on the electron and its acceleration.

In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated from rest through a p.d. of 1500 V between a cathode and an anode 3.0 cm apart. (a) Explain why the speed does not depend on the distance between cathode and anode. (b) The beam then enters a vertical uniform field. Describe the shape of the path in the field. (c) Explain why the electrons travel in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance. (b) Parabolic: constant velocity horizontally, constant acceleration vertically. (c) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter.
items.markingKey: (a) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance [1] (b) parabola [1]; constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration [1] [2] (c) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter [1]

items.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through a p.d. of 200 V. What kinetic energy does it gain?
Explain how a uniform electric field can be used to measure the charge on an oil drop.
items.answer: Adjust the p.d. until the drop is stationary: qV/d = mg. Knowing m (from its terminal velocity) and V, d, the charge q = mgd/V can be found.
items.markingKey: balance: qE = mg [1]; q = mgd/V with m known [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why electrons in a cathode-ray tube can be treated as unaffected by gravity in the deflecting field.
items.answer: The electric force eE is many orders of magnitude greater than the weight mₑg (mass is tiny), so gravity is negligible.
items.markingKey: compare eE with mg [1]; weight negligible [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why electrons in a cathode-ray tube can be treated as unaffected by gravity in the deflecting field. (b) Explain why the kinetic energy gained by a charge accelerated through a p.d. does not depend on the separation of the plates.
items.answer: (a) The electric force eE is many orders of magnitude greater than the weight mₑg (mass is tiny), so gravity is negligible. (b) Work done = qV; a larger separation gives a smaller field (E = V/d) but a longer distance, so qEd = qV is the same.
items.markingKey: (a) compare eE with mg [1]; weight negligible [1] [2] (b) W = qV [1]; E smaller but distance larger [1] [2]

items.stem: An oil drop of mass 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between two horizontal plates 15 mm apart when the p.d. between them is 589 V. Calculate the charge on the drop and the number of excess electrons it carries.
items.answer: q = 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 5 electrons

items.stem: An electron moving horizontally at 3.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ enters the uniform field between two horizontal plates 5.0 cm long and 3.0 cm apart, midway between them. The p.d. between the plates is 200 V. Calculate the time spent between the plates and the vertical acceleration.

In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated from rest through a p.d. of 2000 V between a cathode and an anode 2.0 cm apart. (a) Calculate the speed of the electrons. (b) Explain why the speed does not depend on the distance between cathode and anode. (c) Explain why the electrons travel in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) 2.65 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (b) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance. (c) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter.
items.markingKey: (a) ½mv² = eV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.65 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance [1] (c) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter [1]

items.stem: In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated from rest through a p.d. of 1500 V between a cathode and an anode 2.0 cm apart. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy of each electron leaving the anode. (b) Explain why the speed does not depend on the distance between cathode and anode. (c) The beam then enters a vertical uniform field. Describe the shape of the path in the field. (d) Explain why the electrons travel in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) 2.40 × 10⁻¹⁶ J (b) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance. (c) Parabolic: constant velocity horizontally, constant acceleration vertically. (d) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter.
items.markingKey: (a) Ek = eV: 2.40 × 10⁻¹⁶ J [1] (b) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance [1] (c) parabola [1]; constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration [1] [2] (d) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter [1]

items.stem: Two point charges repel with force F. The distance between them is tripled. The new force is …
items.markingKey: F ∝ 1/r².

items.stem: Explain why the gravitational force between a proton and an electron in an atom can be neglected compared with the electric force.
items.answer: The electric force is about 10³⁹ times larger, because e²/(4πε₀) is enormous compared with Gmₚmₑ; both depend on 1/r² so the ratio is independent of distance.
items.markingKey: ratio ~10³⁹ [1]; same r dependence so ratio fixed [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why there is a point between two positive charges where the electric field strength is zero, and why it is closer to the smaller charge.
items.answer: The fields from the two charges point in opposite directions between them; they cancel where Q₁/r₁² = Q₂/r₂². For the smaller charge to give an equal field, the point must be closer to it.
items.markingKey: fields opposite in direction between charges [1]; equal magnitude closer to smaller charge [1] [2]

items.stem: Two small charged spheres carry charges of +4.5 × 10⁻⁹ C and −2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C. Their centres are 30 cm apart. Determine the force between them.
items.markingKey: F = Qq/(4πε₀r²) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.5 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.30² = 8.99 × 10⁻⁴ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Two small charged spheres carry charges of +4.5 × 10⁻⁹ C and −3.0 × 10⁻⁹ C. Their centres are 15 cm apart. Calculate the force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.
items.answer: 5.40 × 10⁻⁶ N, attractive
items.markingKey: F = Qq/(4πε₀r²) [1]; = 5.40 × 10⁻⁶ N [1]; attractive (opposite charges) [1] [3]

items.stem: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, an electron orbits a proton in a circle of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational force between them. (b) Calculate the speed of the electron, assuming the electric force provides the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: (a) F = Gmₚmₑ/r² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.61 × 10⁻⁴⁷ N [1] [2] (b) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Two point charges repel with force F. The distance between them is tripled. The new force is … (b) What is the constant 1/(4πε₀) approximately equal to?
Derive the expression for the field strength of a point charge from Coulomb's law.
items.answer: Force on test charge q at distance r: F = Qq/(4πε₀r²). E = F/q = Q/(4πε₀r²).
items.markingKey: Coulomb's law for test charge [1]; divide by q [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare the electric field of a point charge with the gravitational field of a point mass.
items.answer: Both are radial and inverse-square (E = Q/4πε₀r², g = GM/r²). Gravitational fields are always attractive (towards the mass); electric fields point away from positive charges and towards negative charges.
items.markingKey: both radial inverse square [1]; attraction only vs attraction/repulsion [1] [2]

items.stem: Two small charged spheres carry charges of +2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C and −6.0 × 10⁻⁹ C. Their centres are 30 cm apart. What is the force between them?
An isolated conducting sphere of radius 20 cm carries a charge of 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ C. Calculate the electric field strength at the surface and at a distance of 60.0 cm from the centre.
An isolated conducting sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ C. Calculate the electric field strength at the surface and at a distance of 40 cm from the centre.

In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, an electron orbits a proton in a circle of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational force between them. (b) Calculate the electric field strength due to the proton at the electron. (c) Calculate the speed of the electron, assuming the electric force provides the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: (a) F = Gmₚmₑ/r² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.61 × 10⁻⁴⁷ N [1] [2] (b) E = e/(4πε₀r²) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.12 × 10¹¹ N C⁻¹ [1] [2] (c) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the definition of electric potential at a point?
options: the work done in moving a charge between two plates
the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point
the force per unit charge at the point
the energy stored per unit volume
items.answer: the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point
items.markingKey: V = W/q from infinity.

items.stem: Explain why the electric potential near an isolated positive charge is positive, whereas gravitational potential is always negative.
items.answer: Potential is zero at infinity. Work must be done against repulsion to bring a positive test charge towards a positive charge, so V is positive; gravity is always attractive so work is done by the field and φ is negative.
items.markingKey: zero at infinity [1]; work done against repulsion vs by attraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the relationship between field lines and equipotential surfaces.
items.answer: Field lines are always perpendicular to equipotentials; no work is done moving along an equipotential, so the field has no component along it. Closely spaced equipotentials indicate a strong field.
items.markingKey: perpendicular [1]; spacing relates to field strength / no work along [1] [2]

items.stem: A point charge of 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is fixed in place. Point A is 5.0 cm from it. Work out the electric potential at A.
items.markingKey: V = Q/(4πε₀r) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 5.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.050 = 899 V. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A point charge of 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is fixed in place. Point A is 5.0 cm and point B is 15.0 cm from it. Calculate the potential at A and at B, and the potential difference between A and B.
items.markingKey: V = Q/4πε₀r [1]; both values [1]; difference 599 V [1] [3]

items.stem: A point charge of −3.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is fixed in place. Point A is 5.0 cm and point B is 15.0 cm from it. (a) Calculate the potential at A and at B. (b) Calculate the work done by an external agent in moving a +5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ C charge from B to A. (c) Explain the sign of your answer to (b).
items.answer: (a) −540 V; −180 V (b) −1.80 × 10⁻⁷ J (c) negative: the field does work (attraction), so the external agent does negative work
items.markingKey: (a) V = Q/4πε₀r: both values [1] (b) W = q(V_A − V_B) [1]; = −1.80 × 10⁻⁷ J [1] (c) sign explained [1] [4]

items.stem: The dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a Bangkok science museum is a sphere of radius 20 cm at a potential of 5.0 × 10⁴ V. (a) Define electric potential at a point. (b) Calculate the charge on the dome.
items.answer: (a) Work done per unit positive charge bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point. (b) 1.11 × 10⁻⁶ C
items.markingKey: (a) work per unit charge [1]; from infinity [1] [2] (b) Q = 4πε₀RV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.11 × 10⁻⁶ C [1] [2]

items.stem: The dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a Dubai science museum is a sphere of radius 10 cm at a potential of 5.0 × 10⁴ V. (a) Calculate the charge on the dome. (b) Calculate the field strength at the surface of the dome. (c) Calculate the energy gained by an electron moving from infinity to the dome surface.
items.markingKey: (a) Q = 4πε₀RV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.56 × 10⁻⁷ C [1] [2] (b) E = V/R for a sphere (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.00 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ [1] [2] (c) W = eV: 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁵ J [1]

items.stem: The electric potential at distance r from a point charge is V. At distance 2r it is …
What is the electric potential energy of two charges Q and q a distance r apart?
items.answer: Qq/(4πε₀r)
items.markingKey: Ep = qV.

items.stem: Explain how the field strength at a point can be found from a graph of potential V against distance r.
items.answer: E = −dV/dr: draw a tangent to the curve at that point; the field strength is minus the gradient.
items.markingKey: tangent gradient [1]; E = −gradient [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of energy, how the distance of closest approach of an α-particle to a nucleus can be found.
items.answer: At closest approach the α-particle is momentarily at rest; its initial kinetic energy has all been converted to electric potential energy: Ek = Qq/(4πε₀r), so r = Qq/(4πε₀Ek).
items.markingKey: KE → electric PE [1]; equation for r [1] [2]

items.stem: A point charge of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ C is fixed in place. Point A is 20 cm from it. What is the electric potential at A?
An α-particle with kinetic energy 5.5 MeV is fired directly at a silver nucleus (proton number 47). Calculate the distance of closest approach.

Two positive point charges of 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C and 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ C are held 20 cm apart. One is released and moves until they are 60.0 cm apart. Calculate the electric potential energy at each separation and the kinetic energy gained by the moving charge.
items.answer: 0.225 J and 0.0749 J; KE gained = 0.150 J
items.markingKey: Ep = Qq/(4πε₀r) [1]; both values [1]; ΔEk = 0.150 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A point charge of −6.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is fixed in place. Point A is 20 cm from it. Calculate the electric potential at A.
items.markingKey: V = Q/(4πε₀r) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × −6.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.20 = −270 V. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A point charge of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ C is fixed in place. Point A is 20 cm and point B is 60.0 cm from it. (a) Calculate the potential at A and at B. (b) Calculate the work done by an external agent in moving a +5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ C charge from B to A. (c) Explain the sign of your answer to (b).
items.answer: (a) 450 V; 150 V (b) 1.50 × 10⁻⁷ J (c) positive: work is done against repulsion
items.markingKey: (a) V = Q/4πε₀r: both values [1] (b) W = q(V_A − V_B) [1]; = 1.50 × 10⁻⁷ J [1] (c) sign explained [1] [4]

items.stem: The dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a Colombo science museum is a sphere of radius 20 cm at a potential of 5.0 × 10⁴ V. (a) Define electric potential at a point. (b) Calculate the potential at a distance of 60.0 cm from the centre.
items.answer: (a) Work done per unit positive charge bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point. (b) 1.67 × 10⁴ V
items.markingKey: (a) work per unit charge [1]; from infinity [1] [2] (b) V ∝ 1/r: 1.67 × 10⁴ V [1]

items.stem: The dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a Bogotá science museum is a sphere of radius 10 cm at a potential of 1.0 × 10⁵ V. (a) Calculate the charge on the dome. (b) Calculate the energy gained by an electron moving from infinity to the dome surface.
items.markingKey: (a) Q = 4πε₀RV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.11 × 10⁻⁶ C [1] [2] (b) W = eV: 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁴ J [1]

items.stem: An electron is placed in an electric field directed to the right. In which direction is the force on the electron?
items.answer: to the left
items.markingKey: Negative charge experiences a force opposite to the field.

items.stem: Describe the electric field pattern for two parallel plates at different potentials, and state what the spacing of the lines indicates.
items.answer: Parallel, equally spaced lines from the positive to the negative plate, curving outwards at the edges; closer lines indicate a stronger field.
items.markingKey: correct shape [1]; correct direction [1] [2]

items.stem: A proton is in a uniform electric field of strength 1.0 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. Determine the magnitude of the electric force on it.
items.markingKey: F = qE = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁵ = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A dust particle with charge 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ C is in a uniform electric field of strength 2.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Calculate the electric force on it and its acceleration (ignore gravity).

A small charged sphere carrying +2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C experiences a force of 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ N when placed at point P near a charged object. (a) Define electric field strength. (b) The sphere is replaced by an electron. Calculate the force on the electron. (c) Show that N C⁻¹ is equivalent to V m⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) Force per unit positive charge on a small test charge. (b) 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, in the opposite direction (c) V m⁻¹ = J C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N m C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N C⁻¹.
items.markingKey: (a) Force per unit positive charge on a small test charge [1] (b) F = eE [1]; opposite direction [1] [2] (c) V = J C⁻¹ [1]; J = N m [1] [2]

items.stem: An electron enters a uniform electric field between horizontal plates, moving horizontally. Its path between the plates is …
items.answer: a parabola
items.markingKey: Constant force perpendicular to initial velocity, like a projectile.

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 2.0 cm apart with a p.d. of 1200 V between them. An electron is between the plates. Work out the electric field strength between the plates.
items.markingKey: E = V/d = 1200/0.020 = 60 000 V m⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An oil drop of mass 6.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between two horizontal plates 10 mm apart when the p.d. between them is 1990 V. Calculate the charge on the drop and the number of excess electrons it carries.
items.answer: q = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 2 electrons

items.stem: In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated from rest through a p.d. of 1500 V between a cathode and an anode 4.0 cm apart. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy of each electron leaving the anode. (b) Calculate the speed of the electrons. (c) The beam then enters a vertical uniform field. items.answer: (a) 2.40 × 10⁻¹⁶ J (b) 2.30 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (c) Parabolic: constant velocity horizontally, constant acceleration vertically. (d) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter.
items.markingKey: (a) Ek = eV: 2.40 × 10⁻¹⁶ J [1] (b) ½mv² = eV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.30 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (c) parabola [1]; constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration [1] [2] (d) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter [1]

Two small charged spheres are held near each other. The charge on one sphere is multiplied by 4 while the separation stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the electrostatic force between them changes.
items.answer: The electrostatic force between them becomes 4 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using F = Qq/(4πε₀r²): electrostatic force between them ∝ charge on one sphere; factor = 4.00 = 4.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Two small charged spheres carry charges of +5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C and −1.0 × 10⁻⁹ C. Their centres are 5.0 cm apart. Calculate the force between them.
items.markingKey: F = Qq/(4πε₀r²) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.050² = 0.0180 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, an electron orbits a proton in a circle of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. (a) Calculate the electric force between the electron and the proton. (b) Calculate the speed of the electron, assuming the electric force provides the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: (a) F = e²/(4πε₀r²) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.19 × 10⁻⁸ N [1] [2] (b) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how the field strength at a point can be found from a graph of potential V against distance r. (b) Explain why the electric potential near an isolated positive charge is positive, whereas gravitational potential is always negative.
items.answer: (a) E = −dV/dr: draw a tangent to the curve at that point; the field strength is minus the gradient. (b) Potential is zero at infinity. Work must be done against repulsion to bring a positive test charge towards a positive charge, so V is positive; gravity is always attractive so work is done by the field and φ is negative.
items.markingKey: (a) tangent gradient [1]; E = −gradient [1] [2] (b) zero at infinity [1]; work done against repulsion vs by attraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain, in terms of energy, how the distance of closest approach of an α-particle to a nucleus can be found. (b) Explain how the field strength at a point can be found from a graph of potential V against distance r.
items.answer: (a) At closest approach the α-particle is momentarily at rest; its initial kinetic energy has all been converted to electric potential energy: Ek = Qq/(4πε₀r), so r = Qq/(4πε₀Ek). (b) E = −dV/dr: draw a tangent to the curve at that point; the field strength is minus the gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) KE → electric PE [1]; equation for r [1] [2] (b) tangent gradient [1]; E = −gradient [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the relationship between field lines and equipotential surfaces. (b) Explain, in terms of energy, how the distance of closest approach of an α-particle to a nucleus can be found.
items.answer: (a) Field lines are always perpendicular to equipotentials; no work is done moving along an equipotential, so the field has no component along it. Closely spaced equipotentials indicate a strong field. (b) At closest approach the α-particle is momentarily at rest; its initial kinetic energy has all been converted to electric potential energy: Ek = Qq/(4πε₀r), so r = Qq/(4πε₀Ek).
items.markingKey: (a) perpendicular [1]; spacing relates to field strength / no work along [1] [2] (b) KE → electric PE [1]; equation for r [1] [2]

items.stem: An α-particle with kinetic energy 4.0 MeV is fired directly at a copper nucleus (proton number 29). Calculate the distance of closest approach.

Two positive point charges of 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C and 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ C are held 25 cm apart. One is released and moves until they are 75 cm apart. Calculate the electric potential energy at each separation and the kinetic energy gained by the moving charge.
items.answer: 0.719 J and 0.240 J; KE gained = 0.480 J
items.markingKey: Ep = Qq/(4πε₀r) [1]; both values [1]; ΔEk = 0.480 J [1] [3]

items.stem: The dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a Lisbon science museum is a sphere of radius 15 cm at a potential of 1.0 × 10⁵ V. (a) Define electric potential at a point. (b) Calculate the field strength at the surface of the dome.
items.answer: (a) Work done per unit positive charge bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point. (b) 6.67 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) work per unit charge [1]; from infinity [1] [2] (b) E = V/R for a sphere (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.67 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: A charge of 4.0 μC experiences a force of 0.020 N in an electric field. What is the field strength?
Describe the electric field pattern for a positive and an equal negative point charge, and state what the spacing of the lines indicates.
items.answer: Lines curve from the positive to the negative charge, densest between them; closer lines indicate a stronger field.
items.markingKey: correct shape [1]; correct direction [1] [2]

items.stem: A dust particle with charge 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ C is in a uniform electric field of strength 5.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Work out the magnitude of the electric force on it.
items.markingKey: F = qE = 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁷ × 5.0 × 10⁴ = 4.00 × 10⁻¹² N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A proton is in a uniform electric field of strength 1.0 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. Calculate the electric force on it and its acceleration (ignore gravity).

A small charged sphere carrying +5.0 × 10⁻⁹ C experiences a force of 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ N when placed at point P near a charged object. (a) Define electric field strength. (b) The sphere is replaced by an electron. Calculate the force on the electron. (c) Show that N C⁻¹ is equivalent to V m⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) Force per unit positive charge on a small test charge. (b) 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁵ N, in the opposite direction (c) V m⁻¹ = J C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N m C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N C⁻¹.
items.markingKey: (a) Force per unit positive charge on a small test charge [1] (b) F = eE [1]; opposite direction [1] [2] (c) V = J C⁻¹ [1]; J = N m [1] [2]

items.stem: The p.d. between two parallel plates is kept constant and the separation is doubled. The field strength …
items.answer: halves
items.markingKey: E = V/d.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the path of an electron moving horizontally into the uniform vertical field between two charged plates is parabolic. (b) Explain how a uniform electric field can be used to measure the charge on an oil drop.
items.answer: (a) The force eE is constant and vertical, so there is constant vertical acceleration; the horizontal velocity is constant (no horizontal force). This is the same as projectile motion, giving a parabola. (b) Adjust the p.d. until the drop is stationary: qV/d = mg. Knowing m (from its terminal velocity) and V, d, the charge q = mgd/V can be found.
items.markingKey: (a) constant vertical force/acceleration [1]; constant horizontal velocity → parabola [1] [2] (b) balance: qE = mg [1]; q = mgd/V with m known [1] [2]

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 2.0 cm apart with a p.d. of 1200 V between them. An electron is between the plates. Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.
items.markingKey: E = V/d = 1200/0.020 = 60 000 V m⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 5.0 cm apart with a p.d. of 5000 V between them. An electron is between the plates. Calculate the field strength, the force on the electron and its acceleration.

In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated from rest through a p.d. of 3000 V between a cathode and an anode 2.0 cm apart. (a) Calculate the speed of the electrons. (b) Explain why the speed does not depend on the distance between cathode and anode. (c) The beam then enters a vertical uniform field. Describe the shape of the path in the field. (d) Explain why the electrons travel in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) 3.25 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (b) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance. (c) Parabolic: constant velocity horizontally, constant acceleration vertically. (d) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter.
items.markingKey: (a) ½mv² = eV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.25 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) The work done (eV) depends only on the p.d.; a larger gap gives a weaker field over a longer distance [1] (c) parabola [1]; constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration [1] [2] (d) So they do not collide with gas molecules and lose energy or scatter [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Outside a charged conducting sphere, the field is the same as that of … (b) Two charges of +Q and −Q are a distance d apart. At the midpoint, the electric field is …
items.answer: (a) a point charge at the centre of the sphere (b) directed towards −Q
items.markingKey: (a) Charge on a sphere acts as if concentrated at the centre for outside points. (b) Both contributions point from + towards −.

items.stem: Two charged polystyrene balls hang near each other on threads. The separation is halved while the charge on one sphere stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the electrostatic force between them changes.
items.answer: The electrostatic force between them becomes 4 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using F = Qq/(4πε₀r²): electrostatic force between them ∝ separation^-2.00; factor = 0.500^-2.00 = 4.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.markingKey: F = Qq/(4πε₀r²) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.5 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.10² = 4.05 × 10⁻⁶ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]
